concepts.title: Protein digestion, zymogen activation, and intestinal uptake
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: The amino acid pool is replenished by dietary protein digestion, body-protein turnover, and synthesis of nonessential amino acids; there is no dedicated storage protein for excess amino acids. Gastric acid denatures proteins, and pepsin begins peptide-bond hydrolysis in the stomach. Intestinal brush-border enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen, and trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen. Most free amino acids enter enterocytes through sodium-coupled secondary active transport, whereas dipeptides and tripeptides use proton-coupled transport. Intracellular peptidases release free amino acids, which leave the basolateral membrane by facilitated transport into portal blood.
keyPoints: Hydrochloric acid denatures protein; pepsin hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen to trypsin.
Trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen and other pancreatic protease zymogens.
Apical free-amino-acid uptake is commonly Na+-coupled; small-peptide uptake is H+-coupled.
Basolateral amino-acid exit uses facilitated transport.
Excess amino acids are degraded after their nitrogen is removed.
clinicalLinks: Pancreatic insufficiency impairs both protein and fat digestion.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 245-249.

concepts.title: Shared amino-acid transporters and cystinuria
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Amino acids use carrier systems with overlapping substrate specificity in the intestine and renal proximal tubule. Cystinuria is a defect of the transporter handling cystine and the dibasic amino acids ornithine, lysine, and arginine. Reduced renal reabsorption increases urinary loss of all four, but poorly soluble cystine is the component that forms stones. Cystinuria is a membrane-transport defect and differs from cystinosis, in which cystine cannot leave lysosomes.
keyPoints: COLA identifies cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine.
Cystinuria affects intestinal uptake and renal proximal-tubule reabsorption.
Cystine precipitation causes recurrent urinary calculi.
Cystinosis is a separate lysosomal cystine-transport disorder.
clinicalLinks: Cystine stones can obstruct the urinary tract; hydration dilutes urinary cystine and reduces its precipitation.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 249-250.

concepts.title: Transamination, PLP, and the ALT/AST reactions
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Aminotransferases reversibly move an amino group from an amino acid to an alpha-keto acid without releasing free ammonia. Most amino groups are collected on alpha-ketoglutarate, producing glutamate, and every aminotransferase requires pyridoxal phosphate derived from vitamin B6. ALT interconverts alanine plus alpha-ketoglutarate with pyruvate plus glutamate, whereas AST interconverts aspartate plus alpha-ketoglutarate with oxaloacetate plus glutamate. The reverse AST reaction supplies aspartate nitrogen to the urea cycle. Plasma ALT is more specific for hepatocellular injury than AST, although the liver contains a larger absolute amount of AST and both enzymes also occur outside the liver.
keyPoints: Transamination exchanges amino groups; it does not directly liberate NH4+.
PLP temporarily accepts nitrogen as pyridoxamine phosphate.
ALT: alanine + alpha-ketoglutarate ⇌ pyruvate + glutamate.
AST: aspartate + alpha-ketoglutarate ⇌ oxaloacetate + glutamate.
ALT has greater liver specificity; AST is also prominent in cardiac and skeletal muscle.
clinicalLinks: Raised serum aminotransferases indicate cell injury, not a measurement of the liver’s synthetic capacity.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 250-252.

concepts.title: Glutamate dehydrogenase releases collected amino nitrogen
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Mitochondrial glutamate dehydrogenase converts glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate while releasing ammonia. Transamination first collects nitrogen on glutamate, so its subsequent oxidative deamination disposes of nitrogen from many different amino acids. The reversible enzyme uses NAD+ mainly for oxidative deamination and NADPH mainly for reductive amination, with direction determined by substrates and redox state. ADP activates the enzyme and GTP inhibits it, favoring carbon-skeleton oxidation when cellular energy is low.
keyPoints: Glutamate dehydrogenase is mitochondrial and prominent in liver and kidney.
Oxidative deamination regenerates alpha-ketoglutarate and releases NH4+.
Transamination followed by oxidative deamination is called transdeamination.
NAD+ favors the oxidative direction; NADPH supports reductive amination.
ADP activates and GTP inhibits glutamate dehydrogenase.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 252-253.

concepts.title: Glutamine and alanine safely carry peripheral nitrogen
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Peripheral tissues avoid releasing large amounts of toxic free ammonia by carrying nitrogen mainly as glutamine or alanine. Glutamine synthetase consumes ATP to add ammonia to glutamate, forming glutamine; hepatic glutaminase hydrolyzes glutamine to release ammonia for urea synthesis. In muscle, ALT transfers amino nitrogen to pyruvate to make alanine, which travels to the liver. Hepatic ALT converts alanine back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis while directing its nitrogen toward urea, completing the glucose–alanine cycle. In kidney, glutamine-derived ammonium is excreted and contributes to acid elimination.
keyPoints: Glutamine synthetase: glutamate + NH4+ + ATP → glutamine + ADP + Pi.
Glutaminase releases glutamine’s amide nitrogen as ammonia.
Alanine transports an amino group and a pyruvate carbon skeleton from muscle to liver.
Glutamine synthesis is a major ammonia-detoxification mechanism in the brain.
Renal NH4+ excretion supports acid–base balance.
clinicalLinks: Hyperammonemia is accompanied by increased glutamine as tissues sequester ammonia.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 253, 256-257.

concepts.title: Urea-cycle reactions, nitrogen sources, and compartments
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: The liver converts nitrogen to urea, the major circulating nonprotein nitrogen end product, and sends it to the kidneys for excretion. One urea nitrogen comes from free ammonia, the other from aspartate, and its carbonyl carbon comes from bicarbonate. In the mitochondrial matrix, carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I forms carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine transcarbamoylase transfers its carbamoyl group to ornithine, forming citrulline. Citrulline enters the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthetase adds aspartate and argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate and arginine. Cytosolic arginase hydrolyzes arginine to urea and ornithine, and ornithine returns to the mitochondrion. Fumarate can become malate and oxaloacetate, linking the urea cycle to the TCA cycle and regeneration of aspartate.
keyPoints: CPS I and ornithine transcarbamoylase are mitochondrial; the other three cycle enzymes are cytosolic.
NH4+ provides the first nitrogen; aspartate provides the second.
Citrulline exits and ornithine reenters the mitochondrion.
Argininosuccinate lyase produces arginine and fumarate.
Arginase produces urea and ornithine.
Urea is synthesized in liver and excreted mainly by kidney.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 253-257.

concepts.title: Urea-cycle energy cost and N-acetylglutamate regulation
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Each turn of the urea cycle consumes three ATP molecules but four high-energy phosphate bonds. CPS I uses two ATP to form carbamoyl phosphate, whereas argininosuccinate synthetase cleaves a third ATP to AMP and pyrophosphate. N-acetylglutamate is the obligatory allosteric activator of mitochondrial CPS I. N-acetylglutamate synthase makes it from glutamate and acetyl-CoA and is stimulated by arginine, connecting increased amino-acid supply to increased nitrogen disposal. Cytosolic CPS II belongs to pyrimidine synthesis, uses glutamine nitrogen, and does not require N-acetylglutamate.
keyPoints: Urea synthesis consumes 3 ATP but 4 high-energy phosphate bonds.
N-acetylglutamate activates CPS I.
Arginine activates N-acetylglutamate synthase.
CPS I uses free ammonia in mitochondria; CPS II uses glutamine in cytosol.
Substrate supply changes flux rapidly, while enzyme induction provides longer-term adaptation.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 253-255.

concepts.title: Hyperammonemia and recognition of urea-cycle defects
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Liver failure, portosystemic shunting, or a urea-cycle defect can prevent adequate ammonia disposal and cause neurotoxicity, cerebral edema, seizures, or coma. Ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency is the most common inherited urea-cycle disorder and is X-linked; the other classic enzyme defects are autosomal recessive. A block before citrulline formation lowers citrulline, whereas argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency raises citrulline and argininosuccinate lyase deficiency raises argininosuccinate. In OTC deficiency, excess carbamoyl phosphate can enter pyrimidine synthesis and increase urinary orotate, unlike a block at CPS I. Arginase deficiency raises arginine and generally produces less severe hyperammonemia than upstream defects. Treatment principles include limiting excess nitrogen intake while preventing catabolism and providing alternative urinary nitrogen excretion, such as phenylacetylglutamine formation from phenylbutyrate-derived phenylacetate.
keyPoints: OTC deficiency is X-linked; other classic urea-cycle enzyme deficiencies are autosomal recessive.
CPS I deficiency: low citrulline without the orotate increase characteristic of OTC deficiency.
OTC deficiency: low citrulline with increased urinary orotate.
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrullinemia.
Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinate accumulation.
Arginase deficiency raises arginine and often has milder hyperammonemia.
clinicalLinks: Increased plasma glutamine accompanies impaired ammonia disposal.
A newborn becoming lethargic after protein feeding warrants consideration of a nitrogen-disposal defect.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 19, pp. 254-260; Chapter 22, pp. 302-303.

concepts.title: Glucogenic and ketogenic amino acids
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: After nitrogen removal, amino-acid carbon skeletons converge on pyruvate, oxaloacetate, alpha-ketoglutarate, succinyl-CoA, fumarate, acetyl-CoA, or acetoacetate. Glucogenic amino acids form pyruvate or TCA-cycle intermediates that can support net glucose production. Ketogenic amino acids form acetyl-CoA or acetoacetate, which cannot yield net glucose in humans. Leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic; isoleucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan have both glucogenic and ketogenic products in Lippincott’s human pathway classification. Valine and methionine are glucogenic because their degradation can produce succinyl-CoA.
keyPoints: Only leucine and lysine are exclusively ketogenic.
Phenylalanine and tyrosine yield fumarate plus acetoacetate.
Isoleucine yields acetyl-CoA plus a precursor of succinyl-CoA.
Valine, isoleucine, methionine, and threonine can form propionyl-CoA, then succinyl-CoA.
Propionyl-CoA conversion requires biotin and vitamin B12.
Alanine becomes pyruvate; aspartate becomes oxaloacetate.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 261-267.

concepts.title: Folate one-carbon units and serine–glycine interconversion
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Tetrahydrofolate carries single-carbon groups in several oxidation states on N5, N10, or both nitrogen atoms. Serine hydroxymethyltransferase uses PLP to convert serine to glycine while transferring a one-carbon unit to THF, forming N5,N10-methylene-THF. This reversible reaction links amino-acid metabolism to one-carbon requirements for nucleotide synthesis. N10-formyl-THF supplies carbons to purines, N5,N10-methylene-THF supports dTMP synthesis, and N5-methyl-THF supports homocysteine remethylation. Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylation reactions and is distinguished from the folate one-carbon pool.
keyPoints: Serine → glycine requires PLP and THF, with THF accepting the one-carbon unit.
N5,N10-methylene-THF is used to convert dUMP to dTMP.
N10-formyl-THF supplies purine ring carbons.
N5-methyl-THF transfers a methyl group through B12 to homocysteine.
Folate deficiency can increase urinary FIGlu after histidine metabolism.
clinicalLinks: Reduced folate availability impairs nucleotide synthesis and causes megaloblastic anemia.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 262-264, 267-268.

concepts.title: Synthesis of nonessential amino acids
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Nonessential amino acids can be synthesized from common metabolic intermediates in adequate amounts under ordinary conditions. Transamination converts pyruvate, oxaloacetate, and alpha-ketoglutarate into alanine, aspartate, and glutamate, respectively. Serine is synthesized from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate, and serine can supply glycine. ATP-dependent amidation makes glutamine from glutamate using free ammonia and asparagine from aspartate using glutamine as the nitrogen donor. Tyrosine depends on phenylalanine hydroxylation, and cysteine depends on sulfur from methionine, so these amino acids become conditionally essential if their precursor supply or conversion is inadequate.
keyPoints: Serine is nonessential in healthy adults and arises from 3-phosphoglycerate.
Alanine/pyruvate, aspartate/oxaloacetate, and glutamate/alpha-ketoglutarate are transamination pairs.
Glutamine synthetase uses free ammonia; asparagine synthetase uses glutamine nitrogen.
Proline is synthesized from glutamate via glutamate semialdehyde.
Phenylalanine hydroxylase requires tetrahydrobiopterin to synthesize tyrosine.
Cysteine synthesis depends on adequate methionine and serine.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 267-269.

concepts.title: Methionine, S-adenosylmethionine, and transsulfuration
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Methionine combines with ATP to form S-adenosylmethionine, the principal activated methyl donor in human metabolism. After methyl donation, S-adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolyzed to homocysteine and adenosine. Homocysteine can be remethylated to methionine by methionine synthase using methylcobalamin and N5-methyl-THF. Alternatively, PLP-dependent cystathionine beta-synthase joins homocysteine to serine, and cystathionine cleavage produces cysteine plus alpha-ketobutyrate. This transsulfuration route transfers methionine sulfur to cysteine while the remaining methionine carbon skeleton can become succinyl-CoA.
keyPoints: SAM is made from methionine and ATP and donates activated methyl groups.
SAM → S-adenosylhomocysteine → homocysteine.
Methionine synthase requires vitamin B12 and N5-methyl-THF.
Cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine cleavage require PLP.
Serine provides the cysteine carbon skeleton; methionine supplies its sulfur.
clinicalLinks: B6, B12, or folate deficiency can increase homocysteine through different metabolic blocks.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 264-265.

concepts.title: Classic phenylketonuria and tetrahydrobiopterin defects
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Classic phenylketonuria results from deficient phenylalanine hydroxylase, which normally converts phenylalanine to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin. Phenylalanine and alternative metabolites accumulate, while tyrosine becomes an essential dietary amino acid. Untreated disease can cause severe neurodevelopmental impairment, seizures, a musty odor, and hypopigmentation. Early, continuing restriction of phenylalanine limits toxicity, but phenylalanine cannot be eliminated because it is itself essential. Defects of BH4 synthesis or regeneration also cause hyperphenylalaninemia and impair dopamine and serotonin synthesis, so phenylalanine restriction alone does not correct their neurotransmitter deficit.
keyPoints: Classic PKU is phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.
BH4 deficiency is a distinct cause of hyperphenylalaninemia.
Tyrosine becomes essential when phenylalanine hydroxylation is blocked.
Phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, and phenyllactate can accumulate.
Dietary phenylalanine is controlled, not eliminated; aspartame supplies phenylalanine.
Maternal hyperphenylalaninemia can harm fetal development even if the fetus does not have PKU.
clinicalLinks: Newborn screening permits treatment before irreversible neurologic injury.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 270-272.

concepts.title: Branched-chain amino acids and maple syrup urine disease
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are branched-chain amino acids whose initial catabolism occurs mainly in peripheral tissues, especially muscle. After PLP-dependent transamination, the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex carries out oxidative decarboxylation. Deficiency of this complex causes maple syrup urine disease, with accumulation of the three amino acids and their corresponding alpha-keto acids. Feeding difficulty, neurologic deterioration, ketoacidosis, and a sweet urine odor are characteristic, and leucine accumulation is especially neurotoxic. Management controls branched-chain amino-acid intake while retaining enough for growth; some variants respond to thiamine.
keyPoints: MSUD is branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, after the transamination step.
The affected amino acids are leucine, isoleucine, and valine.
BCKD requires TPP, lipoate, FAD, NAD+, and CoA.
Leucine is ketogenic; valine is glucogenic; isoleucine is both.
The shared E3 subunit also participates in PDH and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
clinicalLinks: A defect in shared E3 can add lactic acidosis to the MSUD phenotype.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 265-267, 272-273.

concepts.title: Alkaptonuria and albinism affect different tyrosine pathways
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Tyrosine supplies both degradative products and the pigment melanin, so defects in these separate routes have different clinical effects. Alkaptonuria is deficient homogentisate dioxygenase, also called homogentisic acid oxidase, in phenylalanine and tyrosine degradation. Homogentisate accumulates and oxidizes to dark pigment, causing urine darkening on standing, connective-tissue ochronosis, and later arthritis. Tyrosinase-negative oculocutaneous albinism instead blocks melanin synthesis because copper-dependent tyrosinase is absent or defective. Albinism causes reduced pigmentation and ocular abnormalities, without the homogentisate accumulation of alkaptonuria.
keyPoints: Alkaptonuria: homogentisate dioxygenase deficiency.
Alkaptonuria causes darkening urine, ochronosis, and large-joint disease.
Tyrosinase converts tyrosine toward DOPA and melanin.
Tyrosinase-negative oculocutaneous albinism causes deficient skin, hair, and eye pigment.
Albinism has several genetic forms; not every form is tyrosinase deficiency.
clinicalLinks: Albinism can cause photophobia, impaired vision, and increased skin-cancer risk.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 263-264, 273-274.

concepts.title: Homocystinuria: transsulfuration versus remethylation defects
concepts.rationale: Provides the reaction, mechanism, and distinguishing findings needed to reason through retake questions.
concepts.summary: Classic homocystinuria most often reflects cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, which blocks the PLP-dependent entry of homocysteine into transsulfuration. Homocysteine and methionine rise, while cysteine synthesis decreases. Major manifestations include thromboembolism, lens dislocation, long limbs and fingers, and variable neurodevelopmental impairment. Some patients retain enough enzyme function to respond to pyridoxine. Defects in homocysteine remethylation can also raise homocysteine but do not produce the same increased-methionine pattern, so elevated homocysteine alone does not identify the enzyme defect.
keyPoints: Classic homocystinuria is usually autosomal recessive cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency.
CBS deficiency raises homocysteine and methionine and lowers cysteine availability.
CBS requires vitamin B6-derived PLP.
Thrombosis is a major cause of morbidity and early death.
Remethylation requires folate and B12; its failure can raise homocysteine without high methionine.
clinicalLinks: The combination of ectopia lentis, skeletal findings, and thrombosis helps distinguish classic homocystinuria.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 20, pp. 264-265, 273-274.

concepts.title: Heme synthesis links glycine, succinyl-CoA, and iron
concepts.rationale: Heme synthesis requires both cellular compartments and distinct hepatic and erythroid regulatory mechanisms.
concepts.summary: Heme consists of ferrous iron coordinated within protoporphyrin IX and is made chiefly in erythroid precursors and liver. Mitochondrial ALA synthase condenses glycine with succinyl-CoA in the PLP-dependent, committed and rate-limiting reaction. ALA then enters the cytosolic portion of the pathway, whereas the last three reactions occur in mitochondria. Ferrochelatase completes synthesis by inserting Fe2+ into protoporphyrin IX. Hepatic hemin suppresses ALAS1 expression and mitochondrial import, while erythroid ALAS2 production responds to iron availability.
keyPoints: ALA synthase requires pyridoxal phosphate, derived from vitamin B6.
The first and last three reactions are mitochondrial; intervening reactions are cytosolic.
ALA dehydratase joins two ALA molecules to form porphobilinogen.
Four porphobilinogens form hydroxymethylbilane, which becomes uroporphyrinogen III.
Ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX.
Mature erythrocytes cannot synthesize heme because they lack mitochondria.
clinicalLinks: Loss of erythroid ALAS2 activity can cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia.
Drugs that induce hepatic cytochrome P450 can consume heme and increase ALAS1 expression.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 277-281, porphyrin structure, heme synthesis, and Figures 21.3-21.8.

concepts.title: Porphyrias and lead poisoning block different heme-synthesis steps
concepts.rationale: The enzyme, accumulated intermediates, and photosensitivity distinguish the common exam presentations.
concepts.summary: A block in heme synthesis causes accumulation of intermediates upstream of the defective enzyme. Acute intermittent porphyria is caused by hydroxymethylbilane synthase deficiency, also called porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency, and produces neurovisceral attacks without photosensitivity. Porphyria cutanea tarda involves reduced uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase activity and photosensitive skin lesions. Lead directly inhibits both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, reducing heme production and contributing to anemia. Decreased hepatic heme removes feedback suppression of ALAS1, amplifying precursor accumulation.
keyPoints: Acute intermittent porphyria: increased ALA and porphobilinogen, abdominal pain, and neurologic or psychiatric symptoms.
Porphyria cutanea tarda: uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, porphyrin accumulation, and photosensitivity.
Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria.
Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; ALAS1 may increase secondarily.
Heme depletion by enzyme-inducing drugs can precipitate acute hepatic porphyria attacks.
clinicalLinks: Hemin and glucose suppress hepatic ALAS1 and reduce precursor production during acute porphyria attacks.
Iron overload, alcohol, estrogens, and viral infection can contribute to expression of porphyria cutanea tarda.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 279-281, porphyrias and Figure 21.8; p. 290, lead-poisoning study question.

concepts.title: Heme degradation produces bilirubin, urobilin, and stercobilin
concepts.rationale: The sequence explains the pigments measured in blood, urine, and stool.
concepts.summary: Most heme degradation follows removal of aging erythrocytes by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Heme oxygenase uses oxygen and NADPH to open the ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and forming green biliverdin; biliverdin reductase then forms bilirubin. Poorly water-soluble unconjugated bilirubin travels to the liver bound to albumin. Hepatic bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, UGT1A1, adds glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronate, producing water-soluble conjugated bilirubin for secretion into bile. Intestinal bacteria generate urobilinogen, most of which gives rise to brown stercobilin, while a small portion reaches urine and is oxidized to yellow urobilin.
keyPoints: Heme oxygenase opens the porphyrin ring; biliverdin reductase reduces the resulting biliverdin.
Heme oxygenase requires O2 and NADPH and releases CO and Fe2+.
Unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and normally absent from urine.
Conjugated bilirubin can enter urine when its plasma concentration rises.
Stercobilin colors stool brown; urobilin colors urine yellow.
clinicalLinks: Conjugation defects cause unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia; impaired biliary secretion can cause conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 282-284, heme degradation, bilirubin conjugation, and Figures 21.9-21.10.

concepts.title: Jaundice patterns reflect bilirubin production, conjugation, and excretion
concepts.rationale: Fractionated bilirubin and urinary pigments identify the mechanism of jaundice and prevent confusion about neonatal phototherapy.
concepts.summary: Jaundice is yellow discoloration caused by bilirubin accumulation, so plasma bilirubin is the analyte measured directly to assess it. Hemolysis raises bilirubin production and typically increases unconjugated bilirubin and urinary urobilinogen. Hepatocellular injury can impair both conjugation and biliary secretion, creating a mixed pattern, whereas complete extrahepatic obstruction causes predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, bilirubinuria, pale stools, and absent or markedly reduced urinary urobilinogen. Gilbert syndrome causes mild, intermittent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia through reduced UGT1A1 activity. Physiologic neonatal jaundice reflects low conjugating capacity, and indicated phototherapy uses blue light to form more water-soluble bilirubin photoisomers that can be excreted without glucuronidation.
keyPoints: Direct-reacting bilirubin approximates conjugated bilirubin; indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct.
Hemolysis: unconjugated bilirubin rises, urine bilirubin is absent, and urinary urobilinogen increases.
Complete obstruction: conjugated bilirubin rises, urine bilirubin appears, and intestinal and urinary urobilinogen fall.
Hepatocellular jaundice can contain both conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin.
Gilbert syndrome is usually benign and may become apparent with fasting or illness.
Neonatal phototherapy changes bilirubin structure rather than activating hepatic conjugation; severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia can cause kernicterus.
clinicalLinks: Severe loss of bilirubin UGT activity causes Crigler-Najjar syndrome.
Unconjugated bilirubin becomes especially neurotoxic when the albumin-binding capacity is exceeded.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 282-285, bilirubin UGT deficiency, jaundice types, phototherapy, and bilirubin measurement.

concepts.title: Tyrosine supplies dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine
concepts.rationale: The pathway connects precursor amino acids, vitamin-derived cofactors, and clinically useful degradation products.
concepts.summary: Tyrosine is converted to DOPA by tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step in catecholamine synthesis. PLP-dependent decarboxylation of DOPA produces dopamine, which dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts to norepinephrine using copper and ascorbate. Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT) uses S-adenosylmethionine to methylate norepinephrine into epinephrine. Monoamine oxidase and catechol-O-methyltransferase inactivate catecholamines, producing metabolites that are excreted in urine.
keyPoints: Pathway: tyrosine → DOPA → dopamine → norepinephrine → epinephrine.
Tyrosine hydroxylase requires BH4; DOPA decarboxylase requires PLP.
Dopamine beta-hydroxylase requires copper and vitamin C.
SAM provides methyl groups for epinephrine synthesis and COMT reactions.
Vanillylmandelic acid derives from norepinephrine and epinephrine; homovanillic acid derives from dopamine.
clinicalLinks: Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and supplies a dopamine precursor in Parkinson disease.
Catecholamine-producing pheochromocytomas can increase urinary catecholamine metabolites.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 286-288, catecholamine synthesis and degradation, Figures 21.15-21.16.

concepts.title: Histidine and tryptophan supply histamine and serotonin
concepts.rationale: These amines test recognition of amino-acid precursors and the distinction between hydroxylation and decarboxylation.
concepts.summary: Histamine forms by PLP-dependent decarboxylation of histidine. It participates in allergic and inflammatory responses and stimulates gastric acid secretion. Serotonin, or 5-hydroxytryptamine, is made from tryptophan by BH4-dependent hydroxylation followed by PLP-dependent decarboxylation. Serotonin functions in the gut and nervous system, is degraded by monoamine oxidase, and can be converted to melatonin in the pineal gland.
keyPoints: Histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine.
Histamine synthesis removes CO2 and requires vitamin B6-derived PLP.
Tryptophan hydroxylase forms 5-hydroxytryptophan using BH4.
Decarboxylation of 5-hydroxytryptophan forms serotonin.
Serotonin is a precursor of melatonin.
clinicalLinks: Antihistamines act at histamine receptors; blocking synthesis is not their usual mechanism.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors increase serotonin availability in synapses.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 286-288, histamine and serotonin, Figures 21.17-21.18.

concepts.title: Creatine buffers ATP and spontaneously forms creatinine
concepts.rationale: Creatine synthesis, phosphate transfer, and degradation are separate reactions frequently conflated in questions.
concepts.summary: Creatine synthesis uses glycine and the guanidino group of arginine, followed by methylation of guanidinoacetate using S-adenosylmethionine derived from methionine. Liver and kidney participate in synthesis, and muscle accumulates creatine as a rapidly available energy buffer. Creatine kinase reversibly transfers phosphate between ATP and creatine, so phosphocreatine can immediately donate phosphate to ADP when ATP demand rises. Creatine and phosphocreatine undergo spontaneous nonenzymatic cyclization to creatinine, which is excreted in urine. Creatinine production therefore depends on muscle mass, while its blood concentration also depends on renal removal.
keyPoints: Creatine precursor amino acids are arginine, glycine, and methionine.
SAM supplies the methyl group; methionine contributes indirectly through SAM.
Creatine + ATP ⇌ phosphocreatine + ADP is catalyzed by creatine kinase.
Phosphocreatine buffers ATP during abrupt increases in muscle energy demand.
Creatinine forms spontaneously rather than through a dedicated degradative enzyme.
Reduced muscle mass can lower creatinine production; reduced kidney clearance can raise plasma creatinine.
clinicalLinks: Creatine kinase in plasma can indicate tissue injury; creatinine is used to assess renal function in the context of muscle mass.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 286-288, creatine synthesis and degradation, Figure 21.19.

concepts.title: Melanin synthesis uses tyrosine and tyrosinase
concepts.rationale: The shared tyrosine precursor does not make the melanin and catecholamine pathways enzymatically identical.
concepts.summary: Melanocytes synthesize melanin from tyrosine to provide pigment in skin, hair, and eyes and to help protect tissues from sunlight. Copper-containing tyrosinase initiates this pathway by converting tyrosine toward DOPA and oxidized intermediates that form melanin. Tyrosinase is distinct from the BH4-dependent tyrosine hydroxylase used in catecholamine synthesis. Defects in melanin production cause forms of oculocutaneous albinism, including tyrosinase-deficient disease.
keyPoints: Tyrosine is the amino-acid precursor of melanin.
Tyrosinase is a copper-containing enzyme in melanocytes.
Melanin contributes pigmentation and protection against solar radiation.
Albinism results from impaired melanin synthesis; it is not synonymous with loss of melanocytes.
clinicalLinks: Reduced pigment in albinism increases susceptibility to sunlight-related skin injury and is associated with ocular abnormalities.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 21, pp. 286-288, melanin; Chapter 20, p. 273, albinism.

Uroporphyrin accumulation and photosensitive skin lesions

concepts.title: De novo purine synthesis builds the ring on PRPP
concepts.rationale: IMP formation and ring donors distinguish the purine pathway from pyrimidine synthesis.
concepts.summary: Purine synthesis assembles the ring on ribose phosphate supplied by PRPP, producing inosine monophosphate as the first completed purine nucleotide. Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the committed step and is inhibited by the end products AMP and GMP. Ring atoms come from glycine, glutamine, aspartate, CO2, and two formyl groups carried by tetrahydrofolate. IMP branches to AMP and GMP, with GTP supporting AMP synthesis and ATP supporting GMP synthesis. Mycophenolic acid inhibits IMP dehydrogenase, blocking the conversion of IMP toward GMP.
keyPoints: PRPP synthetase activates ribose 5-phosphate; its reaction is not the purine-specific committed step.
IMP is the first fully formed purine nucleotide and contains hypoxanthine.
Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase is stimulated by PRPP and inhibited by AMP and GMP.
Glycine donates atoms to purines, but not to the pyrimidine ring.
Glutamine, aspartate, and CO2 contribute to both purine and pyrimidine rings.
Mycophenolate acts through mycophenolic acid to inhibit IMP dehydrogenase and guanine nucleotide synthesis.
clinicalLinks: Rapidly dividing cells are vulnerable to drugs that reduce nucleotide production.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, pp. 293-296, de novo purine synthesis and regulation; pp. 305-306, study question 22.3 on mycophenolic acid.

concepts.title: Purine salvage conserves bases and restrains urate production
concepts.rationale: HGPRT loss explains both the biochemical abnormalities and the characteristic Lesch-Nyhan presentation.
concepts.summary: Purine salvage attaches preformed bases to ribose phosphate donated by PRPP. HGPRT converts hypoxanthine to IMP and guanine to GMP, whereas APRT salvages adenine to AMP. Near-complete HGPRT deficiency causes X-linked Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Failed salvage leaves more bases for degradation and raises PRPP while lowering feedback inhibition by purine nucleotides, increasing de novo synthesis and uric acid production.
keyPoints: HGPRT salvages hypoxanthine and guanine; APRT salvages adenine.
Both phosphoribosyltransferases use PRPP.
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome results from severe HGPRT deficiency.
Increased PRPP and reduced IMP/GMP feedback drive additional purine synthesis.
Hyperuricemia, uric acid stones, motor dysfunction, and self-injurious behavior are characteristic.
clinicalLinks: Lowering urate addresses the metabolic complication of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome but does not correct its neurologic phenotype.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, p. 296, purine salvage and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, Figures 22.10-22.11.

concepts.title: Purine degradation and renal handling determine urate levels
concepts.rationale: Urate excess, xanthine oxidase inhibition, and renal urate wasting require different mechanisms.
concepts.summary: Human purine degradation ends in uric acid, which is predominantly present as urate at physiologic pH. Xanthine oxidase catalyzes hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid; humans do not further convert uric acid to allantoin. Hyperuricemia can reflect increased purine turnover or synthesis, but reduced renal excretion is the more common mechanism. Gout occurs when monosodium urate crystals deposit and trigger inflammation; allopurinol and its metabolite oxypurinol inhibit xanthine oxidase and lower urate production. Conversely, generalized proximal tubular dysfunction in Fanconi syndrome can increase renal urate loss and cause hypouricemia.
keyPoints: Purine breakdown ends at uric acid in humans.
Xanthine oxidase produces uric acid and is inhibited by allopurinol/oxypurinol.
Gout crystals are needle-shaped monosodium urate with negative birefringence.
Hyperuricemia alone does not establish gout.
Purine overproduction and renal underexcretion both raise urate.
Fanconi syndrome can cause renal urate wasting through impaired tubular reabsorption.
clinicalLinks: High cell turnover can increase uric acid production and promote gout or urate stones.
Uricosuric drugs increase renal urate excretion, whereas xanthine oxidase inhibitors reduce its production.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, pp. 298-301, purine degradation, hyperuricemia, gout, and xanthine oxidase inhibitors.

concepts.title: Ribonucleotide reductase supplies deoxyribonucleotides for DNA
concepts.rationale: The substrate level, reducing power, allosteric control, and drug target are central distinctions from thymidylate synthesis.
concepts.summary: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleoside diphosphates into their corresponding deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates by reducing the sugar 2′-hydroxyl group. It acts on both purine and pyrimidine substrates, connecting RNA-type precursors to DNA synthesis. Thioredoxin transfers reducing equivalents to the enzyme and is regenerated using NADPH. ATP activates overall enzyme activity, whereas excessive dATP inhibits it; additional specificity sites help balance individual deoxyribonucleotide pools. Hydroxyurea inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and reduces the supply of DNA precursors.
keyPoints: Substrates are ADP, GDP, CDP, and UDP; products are dADP, dGDP, dCDP, and dUDP.
NADPH supplies the ultimate reducing power through thioredoxin.
dATP inhibits overall reductase activity; ATP activates it.
Hydroxyurea targets ribonucleotide reductase rather than thymidylate synthase.
clinicalLinks: Excess dATP in adenosine deaminase deficiency can block deoxyribonucleotide production.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, pp. 297-298, ribonucleotide reductase, allosteric regulation, and hydroxyurea.

concepts.title: ADA deficiency injures developing lymphocytes
concepts.rationale: The link between toxic purine metabolites and DNA synthesis explains combined immunodeficiency.
concepts.summary: Adenosine deaminase normally participates in degradation of adenosine and deoxyadenosine. Its deficiency permits these metabolites and their phosphorylated derivatives to accumulate, including dATP. High dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, disrupting DNA precursor production, while accumulated purine metabolites also promote lymphocyte developmental arrest and apoptosis. Severe untreated ADA deficiency therefore causes combined immunodeficiency with profound reduction of T, B, and natural killer lymphocytes.
keyPoints: ADA deficiency causes accumulation of adenosine, deoxyadenosine, and dATP.
dATP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and impairs DNA synthesis.
Severe ADA-deficient SCID affects T, B, and NK lineages.
The characteristic blood finding is severe lymphopenia rather than lymphocytosis.
ADA-deficient SCID is inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder.
clinicalLinks: Affected infants are vulnerable to severe infections; enzyme replacement, hematopoietic transplantation, and gene therapy address the underlying deficiency.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, p. 301, adenosine deaminase deficiency and severe combined immunodeficiency.

concepts.title: Pyrimidines are assembled before attachment to ribose
concepts.rationale: The pathway distinguishes CPS II from CPS I and explains orotic aciduria and soluble degradation products.
concepts.summary: Pyrimidine synthesis builds the ring from aspartate and carbamoyl phosphate before attaching it to the ribose phosphate of PRPP. Cytosolic carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II uses glutamine nitrogen and CO2 and is inhibited by UTP and activated by PRPP. Orotate is attached to PRPP to form OMP and then decarboxylated to UMP by the two activities of UMP synthase. UMP supplies UDP and UTP, and glutamine-dependent amination of UTP forms CTP. Pyrimidine nucleoside kinases salvage uridine, cytidine, and thymidine; degradation of pyrimidine rings instead yields soluble beta-alanine or beta-aminoisobutyrate, with release of ammonia and CO2.
keyPoints: Pyrimidine ring donors are aspartate, glutamine, and CO2; glycine is not a donor.
CPS II is cytosolic and uses glutamine; urea-cycle CPS I is mitochondrial and uses free ammonia.
Pyrimidine synthesis is predominantly cytosolic, with dihydroorotate dehydrogenase associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane.
UMP synthase combines orotate phosphoribosyltransferase and OMP decarboxylase activities.
Hereditary orotic aciduria from UMP synthase deficiency can be treated with uridine to bypass the block.
CMP and UMP yield beta-alanine; TMP yields beta-aminoisobutyrate rather than uric acid.
clinicalLinks: UMP synthase deficiency causes orotic aciduria and megaloblastic anemia without the hyperammonemia expected in OTC deficiency.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, pp. 302-304, pyrimidine synthesis, degradation, salvage, and Figure 22.21; pp. 305-306, study question 22.4.

concepts.title: Folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis explains key drug targets
concepts.rationale: Separating thymidylate synthase, DHFR, and bacterial folate synthesis prevents common pharmacology errors.
concepts.summary: Thymidylate synthase converts dUMP to dTMP using N5,N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate, which is oxidized to dihydrofolate during the reaction. Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate, sustaining both thymidylate and purine synthesis. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, whereas the active 5-fluorouracil metabolite FdUMP forms a stable inhibitory complex with thymidylate synthase. Bacteria also require de novo folate synthesis: sulfamethoxazole competes with PABA at dihydropteroate synthase, and trimethoprim inhibits bacterial dihydrofolate reductase.
keyPoints: Thymidylate synthase: dUMP → dTMP using N5,N10-methylene-THF.
Methotrexate inhibits DHFR and decreases reduced folate availability.
5-FU is converted to FdUMP, which inhibits thymidylate synthase.
Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, not DHFR.
Trimethoprim inhibits bacterial DHFR.
Humans obtain folate from diet and lack the bacterial pathway that assembles folate from PABA.
clinicalLinks: Rapidly proliferating marrow and intestinal cells are particularly susceptible to impaired nucleotide synthesis.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 22, pp. 293-295, Figure 22.7 on sulfonamides and antifolates; pp. 303-304, thymidylate synthase, methotrexate, and 5-fluorouracil.

concepts.title: Insulin biosynthesis and glucose-stimulated secretion
concepts.rationale: Essential endocrine physiology with strong tracked-bank coverage, but no dedicated local Chapter 23 teacher deck was located.
concepts.summary: Preproinsulin becomes proinsulin and then insulin plus C-peptide in secretory granules. Beta-cell glucose metabolism raises ATP, closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarizes the membrane, and opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels to trigger exocytosis. Endogenous insulin secretion releases equimolar C-peptide, unlike injected insulin.

Ca2+ triggers granule release
C-peptide marks endogenous secretion

concepts.title: Insulin receptor signaling and metabolic effects
concepts.rationale: This explains the coordinated fed-state response rather than reducing insulin to glucose uptake alone.
concepts.summary: The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase that signals through IRS proteins, PI3K, and Akt. Insulin recruits GLUT4 to skeletal-muscle and adipose membranes and promotes glycogen, lipid, and protein synthesis while suppressing gluconeogenesis and lipolysis. Liver uses GLUT2 rather than insulin-recruited GLUT4, but insulin still changes hepatic enzyme activity and gene expression.

GLUT4 is in muscle and adipose tissue
Insulin promotes storage and synthesis
Insulin suppresses hepatic glucose output

concepts.title: Glucagon signaling and counterregulatory hormones
concepts.rationale: The insulin-glucagon ratio is the main endocrine switch for fed versus fasting metabolism.
concepts.summary: Glucagon binds a hepatic Gs-coupled receptor, raises cAMP, and activates PKA to promote glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis while suppressing glycolysis. Skeletal muscle lacks a meaningful glucagon response and mobilizes glycogen mainly through epinephrine and contraction signals. Glucagon and epinephrine provide rapid defense against falling glucose, with cortisol and growth hormone acting more slowly.

Primary target is liver
No direct glucagon-driven muscle glycogenolysis
Counterregulation protects against hypoglycemia

concepts.title: Hypoglycemia recognition, mechanism, and biochemical diagnosis
concepts.rationale: The active August 25 scope explicitly includes hypoglycemia, and a physician must distinguish autonomic warning symptoms from neuroglycopenia while using the insulin–C-peptide pattern to identify endogenous insulin secretion.
concepts.summary: Falling plasma glucose first triggers counterregulatory hormones and autonomic symptoms such as tremor, palpitations, anxiety, and sweating; more severe or prolonged deficiency deprives the brain of fuel and causes confusion, abnormal behavior, seizures, or coma. Ethanol can cause fasting hypoglycemia because its high NADH state diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, limiting gluconeogenesis. During hypoglycemia, high insulin with high C-peptide supports endogenous secretion, whereas injected insulin raises insulin but suppresses C-peptide.
keyPoints: Autonomic symptoms are early warning signs
Neuroglycopenia causes confusion, seizures, and coma
Ethanol inhibits gluconeogenesis through a high-NADH redox shift
C-peptide distinguishes endogenous from injected insulin
Interpret insulin and C-peptide only in the context of documented low glucose

concepts.title: Absorptive-state metabolism by organ
concepts.rationale: This is the core integrative map for postprandial biochemistry, although no local dedicated Chapter 24 teacher deck was found.
concepts.summary: After a carbohydrate-containing meal, high insulin and low glucagon promote hepatic glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, fatty-acid synthesis, and TAG export. Adipose tissue increases GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake and TAG storage, while muscle takes up glucose and amino acids for glycogen and protein synthesis. Brain primarily uses glucose, and RBCs always rely on glycolysis.

Liver stores glucose and makes lipid
Adipose stores TAG
Muscle makes glycogen and protein
RBCs remain glycolytic

concepts.title: Early fasting: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
concepts.rationale: The timing and changing source of blood glucose are essential to interpreting fasting physiology.
concepts.summary: In early fasting, lower insulin and higher glucagon cause hepatic glycogenolysis to maintain blood glucose. As hepatic glycogen wanes, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids becomes dominant. Adipose lipolysis supplies fatty acids for tissue and hepatic energy plus glycerol for glucose synthesis.

Gluconeogenesis rises with fasting duration
Lipolysis supplies fatty acids and glycerol
Liver preserves glucose for dependent tissues

concepts.title: Prolonged fasting and protein-sparing ketone adaptation
concepts.rationale: This explains why starvation is not simply prolonged early fasting.
concepts.summary: With prolonged fasting, hepatic ketone production rises and the brain increasingly oxidizes ketones. This reduces the brain's glucose demand and therefore decreases the amount of amino acid that must be sacrificed for gluconeogenesis. RBCs still require glucose and produce lactate because they lack mitochondria.

Ketones spare muscle protein

concepts.title: Tissue-specific fuel constraints
concepts.rationale: The exceptions—RBC, liver, brain, muscle, and adipose—are the fastest way to reason through integrated metabolism questions.
concepts.summary: RBCs lack mitochondria and need glucose for glycolysis. Liver can oxidize fatty acids and make ketones but cannot use ketones because it lacks thiophorase; muscle uses fatty acids and ketones according to state. Brain normally relies on glucose but uses substantial ketones during prolonged fasting, while long-chain fatty acids do not cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently.

Liver: produces ketones
Brain: glucose, then more ketones in fasting
Muscle: flexible fuel use

concepts.title: Late starvation shifts muscle away from ketones
concepts.rationale: Adds the specific mechanism needed by retake questions that is absent from the existing chapter concepts.
concepts.summary: Resting skeletal muscle relies increasingly on fatty acids as insulin falls during fasting. It can use both fatty acids and ketone bodies early in starvation, but after prolonged starvation it reduces ketone consumption and uses fatty acids as its principal fuel. This leaves more circulating ketones available to the brain. As brain glucose demand falls, the requirement for gluconeogenesis from muscle amino acids also decreases.
keyPoints: Resting muscle favors fatty acids during prolonged starvation.
Late reduction in muscle ketone use helps preserve ketones for the brain.
Brain ketone use reduces the need for muscle-protein breakdown.
These resting-starvation adaptations do not describe all exercise intensities.

concepts.title: Type 1 versus type 2 diabetes pathophysiology
concepts.rationale: Diabetes is indispensable medical biochemistry, but no dedicated local teacher diabetes deck was located.
concepts.summary: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency. Early type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, followed by progressive beta-cell failure. Both increase hepatic glucose output and impair peripheral glucose handling, but severe unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis are characteristic of untreated type 1 disease.
keyPoints: Type 1: absolute insulin deficiency
Type 2: insulin resistance plus beta-cell dysfunction
Both cause hyperglycemia
Type 1 has greater DKA risk

concepts.title: Diagnosis and glycemic monitoring
concepts.rationale: Every physician must interpret fasting glucose and HbA1c, though thresholds should be checked against current clinical standards when used in practice.
concepts.summary: Diabetes can be diagnosed with reproducibly elevated fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, oral-glucose-tolerance values, or classic symptoms with a high random glucose. HbA1c reflects nonenzymatic glycation over the approximate lifespan of circulating RBCs and therefore represents roughly two to three months of glycemia. Altered RBC survival can make HbA1c misleading.

concepts.title: DKA versus hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
concepts.rationale: This distinction is urgent clinical pattern recognition grounded in the biochemistry of insulin deficiency.
concepts.summary: Severe insulin deficiency activates adipose lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, causing DKA with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. HHS typically retains enough insulin to restrain major ketogenesis but not enough to prevent profound hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis. Both cause dehydration and require urgent fluid, electrolyte, and insulin management.

concepts.rationale: Glycation and polyol-pathway injury connect persistent hyperglycemia to the organs physicians monitor.

Sorbitol accumulation and oxidative stress contribute in tissues with insulin-independent glucose uptake. These mechanisms participate in retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and accelerated atherosclerosis.

concepts.rationale: These signals explain energy-homeostasis feedback and why common obesity usually is not simple leptin deficiency.

concepts.title: Essential fatty acids, limiting amino acids, and nitrogen balance
concepts.rationale: These concepts identify what diet must supply and how protein adequacy is assessed.
concepts.summary: Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are the parent essential fatty acids because humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9. A limiting amino acid is the essential amino acid present in the lowest amount relative to need. concepts.title: Nucleosides, nucleotides, and the phosphodiester backbone
concepts.rationale: The teacher DNA-structure deck explicitly tests the chemical vocabulary needed for every later molecular-biology mechanism.
concepts.summary: A nucleoside is a nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar, whereas a nucleotide adds one or more phosphates. Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine, and uracil. Within one nucleic-acid strand, the 3′ hydroxyl of one sugar is joined to the 5′ phosphate of the next nucleotide by a phosphodiester bond, giving the strand directionality.
keyPoints: Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.
Ribose has a 2′-OH, whereas deoxyribose has 2′-H.
A and G are purines; C, T, and U are pyrimidines.
The backbone linkage is 3′→5′ phosphodiester, and sequences are written 5′→3′.
clinicalLinks: Nucleoside and nucleotide analogs are used as antiviral and anticancer drugs because they can inhibit polymerases or terminate chains.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA)Structure (2).pdf, pp. 6-14 and 25-28.
Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6e, Chapter 29, DNA primary structure and polarity.

concepts.title: Complementary antiparallel DNA, helix forms, and melting
concepts.rationale: Base pairing, strand orientation, and GC-dependent stability are explicit teacher-slide facts and essential for replication, PCR, and hybridization.
concepts.summary: Double-stranded DNA contains complementary strands running in opposite 5′→3′ directions. Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs with cytosine through three, so Chargaff's relation is A = T and G = C. B-DNA is the usual right-handed physiologic form; heat, extreme pH, or low ionic strength denatures DNA, and greater GC content generally raises its melting temperature.
keyPoints: The strands are complementary and antiparallel.
A–T has two hydrogen bonds; G–C has three.
Base stacking also makes a major contribution to duplex stability.
B-DNA is physiologic and right-handed; Z-DNA is left-handed.
Denaturation is strand separation without backbone hydrolysis and can be reversed by controlled annealing.
clinicalLinks: Hybridization-based diagnostics and PCR primer design depend on complementarity and melting temperature.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA)Structure (2).pdf, pp. 22-34.
Lippincott 6e, Chapter 29, DNA secondary structure, denaturation, and A/B/Z forms.

concepts.title: Nucleosomes, histone H1, and chromatin accessibility
concepts.rationale: The complete nucleosome model and the effect of histone acetylation are explicitly covered in the DNA-structure slides and recur in gene regulation.
concepts.summary: A nucleosome core contains two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 around which DNA is wrapped. Histone H1 binds linker DNA and promotes higher-order compaction but is not part of the core octamer. Acetylation of lysine residues reduces histone positive charge, loosens DNA association, and generally makes chromatin more transcriptionally accessible.
keyPoints: Core octamer = 2 × H2A, H2B, H3, and H4.
Histones bind negatively charged DNA because they are rich in lysine and arginine.
H1 is the linker histone.
Open euchromatin is generally more transcriptionally active than compact heterochromatin.
Histone-tail modifications can recruit proteins that activate or repress genes.
clinicalLinks: Histone deacetylase inhibitors are used in selected malignancies because chromatin state can alter gene expression.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA)Structure (2).pdf, pp. 40-43.

concepts.title: Semiconservative, bidirectional replication from origins
concepts.rationale: The replication deck begins with these organizing principles; without them, the enzyme details become disconnected memorization.
concepts.summary: DNA replication is semiconservative because each daughter duplex retains one parental strand and contains one newly synthesized strand. Replication starts at defined origins and usually proceeds bidirectionally through replication forks. Eukaryotic chromosomes use many licensed origins so their large linear genomes can be copied completely during S phase.
keyPoints: Each parental strand is a template for a complementary daughter strand.
An origin opens into a replication bubble with two forks.
Bacterial chromosomes usually use one main origin; eukaryotic chromosomes use many.
Origin firing is restricted so each segment is copied once per cell cycle.
clinicalLinks: Replication stress and defective origin control contribute to genomic instability in cancer.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, slides 3-11 and 53-54.
Lippincott 6e, Chapter 29, semiconservative and bidirectional replication.

concepts.title: Helicase, single-strand binding proteins, and topoisomerases
concepts.rationale: These proteins solve the three immediate physical problems created when a fork opens: strand separation, reannealing, and torsional stress.
concepts.summary: Helicase separates parental strands, while single-strand DNA-binding proteins keep the templates apart and protect them. Unwinding produces positive supercoiling ahead of the fork, which topoisomerases relieve by transiently breaking and resealing DNA. Type I topoisomerases cut one strand without ATP, whereas type II enzymes cut both strands and require ATP.
keyPoints: DnaB is the principal bacterial replicative helicase.
SSB prevents reannealing and protects exposed single-stranded DNA.
Topoisomerase I changes linking number in steps of one.
Topoisomerase II changes linking number in steps of two and includes bacterial DNA gyrase.
clinicalLinks: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial gyrase/topoisomerase IV; several anticancer drugs target human topoisomerases.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, slides 15 onward in the fork-machinery block.

concepts.title: 5′→3′ synthesis, primers, and leading versus lagging strands
concepts.rationale: This is the central mechanistic distinction in DNA replication and is repeatedly tested in both teacher and textbook material.
concepts.summary: DNA polymerases add nucleotides only to a free 3′-OH, so every new strand grows 5′→3′ and requires a primer. The leading strand is synthesized continuously toward the fork, whereas the lagging strand is synthesized away from the fork as Okazaki fragments. Primase makes the RNA primers, and the repeated primers on the lagging strand must later be removed and the fragments joined.
keyPoints: Polymerase reads template 3′→5′ while synthesizing 5′→3′.
A primer supplies the initial paired 3′-OH.
Leading synthesis is continuous; lagging synthesis is discontinuous.
Okazaki fragments arise from antiparallel template geometry.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, strand-synthesis and Okazaki-fragment slides.

concepts.title: Polymerase specialization, proofreading, primer removal, and ligation
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck explicitly contrasts polymerase functions and exonuclease directions, a common source of exam errors.
concepts.summary: Replicative polymerases extend DNA processively, and their 3′→5′ exonuclease activity removes a newly misincorporated nucleotide for proofreading. In bacteria, DNA polymerase I uses 5′→3′ exonuclease activity to remove RNA primers and fills the resulting gaps with DNA. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick by creating the final phosphodiester bond.
keyPoints: Bacterial DNA polymerase III performs most fork elongation.
Proofreading exonuclease is 3′→5′.
Bacterial DNA polymerase I removes primers with 5′→3′ exonuclease.
DNA ligase seals, but does not fill, a nick.
PCNA is the eukaryotic sliding clamp.
clinicalLinks: Polymerase proofreading defects produce mutator phenotypes and increase cancer susceptibility.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, polymerase, exonuclease, and ligase block.

concepts.title: Eukaryotic polymerases and the telomere end-replication problem
concepts.rationale: The replication slides explicitly test polymerase-α/primase, PCNA, mitochondrial polymerase, and telomerase.
concepts.summary: In eukaryotes, polymerase α works with primase to initiate synthesis, while high-processivity polymerases extend the leading and lagging strands with PCNA as their clamp. Linear chromosome ends cannot be completely copied by ordinary lagging-strand synthesis, causing telomere shortening in most somatic cells. Telomerase solves this problem using an intrinsic RNA template and a reverse-transcriptase protein subunit to extend the 3′ chromosome end.
keyPoints: Polymerase α/primase initiates; polymerases ε and δ perform most nuclear elongation.
Polymerase γ replicates mitochondrial DNA.
Telomerase contains RNA plus telomerase reverse transcriptase.
Telomerase is active in germ/stem cells and commonly reactivated in cancer.
Progressive telomere shortening contributes to replicative senescence.
clinicalLinks: Telomerase reactivation supports unlimited proliferation in many cancers.
Telomere-maintenance defects cause bone-marrow failure and other telomere biology disorders.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Deoxyribonucleic Acid(DNA Replication (1).pptx, eukaryotic polymerase and telomere sections.

concepts.title: Mismatch, nucleotide-excision, and base-excision repair
concepts.rationale: The repair pathways link a specific lesion to a specific correction mechanism and to classic inherited cancer syndromes.
concepts.summary: Mismatch repair removes replication errors that escape proofreading. Nucleotide-excision repair removes a short oligonucleotide containing a bulky, helix-distorting lesion such as a UV-induced pyrimidine dimer. Base-excision repair begins with a lesion-specific glycosylase that removes a damaged base, followed by AP-site incision, gap filling, and ligation.
keyPoints: Mismatch repair corrects base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops.
NER handles bulky, helix-distorting lesions.
BER handles small, nonbulky base damage such as deamination.
All three pathways use an intact complementary strand as sequence information.
clinicalLinks: Mismatch-repair defects cause Lynch syndrome and microsatellite instability.
NER defects cause xeroderma pigmentosum with extreme UV sensitivity and early skin cancers.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 29, DNA repair section: mismatch, nucleotide-excision, and base-excision repair.

concepts.title: Homologous recombination versus nonhomologous end joining
concepts.rationale: Double-strand-break pathway choice explains chromosomal rearrangements, radiosensitivity, and BRCA-associated cancer risk.
concepts.summary: Homologous recombination repairs a double-strand break using a homologous template, usually the sister chromatid, and is therefore relatively accurate. Nonhomologous end joining directly processes and ligates broken ends without requiring a homologous template, so sequence may be lost or altered. Failure or misuse of either pathway creates chromosome instability and can initiate malignancy.
keyPoints: HR is template directed and favored in S/G2 when a sister chromatid is available.
NHEJ is available more broadly but is intrinsically error prone.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 participate in homologous recombination.
End-joining errors can create deletions and translocations.
clinicalLinks: BRCA1/2 loss increases breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancer risk.
HR-deficient tumors can be selectively vulnerable to PARP inhibition.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 29, double-strand break repair by HR and NHEJ.

concepts.title: RNA types and bacterial versus eukaryotic mRNA architecture
concepts.rationale: The transcription teacher deck begins by distinguishing RNA products, and those structures determine later processing and translation.
concepts.summary: mRNA carries coding information, tRNA is the adaptor that matches codons to amino acids, and rRNA provides structural and catalytic functions in ribosomes. Bacterial mRNA is often polycistronic and can be translated while it is transcribed. Eukaryotic mRNA is usually monocistronic and is processed with a 5′ cap, splicing, and a 3′ poly(A) tail before export to the cytoplasm.
keyPoints: mRNA is the translated RNA; tRNA decodes; rRNA forms the catalytic ribosome.
RNA uses ribose and uracil and is usually single stranded.
Bacterial transcription and translation can be coupled.
Eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus before translation.

concepts.title: Primer-independent bacterial transcription initiation
concepts.rationale: RNA polymerase, sigma factor, and the −10/−35 promoter are explicit high-yield teacher-slide targets.
concepts.summary: RNA polymerase can begin RNA synthesis de novo and therefore does not require a primer. In bacteria, the sigma factor joins the core enzyme to form a holoenzyme that recognizes promoter consensus sequences. The −35 region supports recognition and the AT-rich −10 Pribnow box facilitates local DNA opening near the +1 start site.
keyPoints: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA 5′→3′ without a primer.
Sigma confers promoter specificity but is not the elongating catalytic core.
Canonical bacterial promoter elements are near −35 and −10.
Promoter sequences are not themselves transcribed.
clinicalLinks: Rifampicin selectively inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase and is central to tuberculosis therapy.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Transcription 2025.pptx, bacterial RNA polymerase and promoter-initiation block.
Lippincott 6e, Chapter 30, bacterial promoter recognition and sigma factor.

concepts.title: Transcript direction, coding/template strands, and bacterial termination
concepts.rationale: Directionality and rho-dependent versus intrinsic termination are repeatedly contrasted in the teacher deck.
concepts.summary: RNA polymerase reads the DNA template strand 3′→5′ and synthesizes RNA 5′→3′. The RNA sequence is complementary to the template and matches the coding strand except that uracil replaces thymine. Intrinsic termination uses a GC-rich RNA hairpin followed by uridines, whereas rho-dependent termination uses an ATP-dependent helicase to release the transcript.
keyPoints: RNA grows 5′→3′ and the template is read 3′→5′.
Coding-strand sequence corresponds to RNA with T replaced by U.
Sigma commonly dissociates after promoter clearance.
Intrinsic termination requires a hairpin plus a U-rich tract.
Rho binds RNA and catches a paused polymerase.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Transcription 2025.pptx, elongation and termination sections.
Lippincott 6e, Chapter 30, transcript directionality and bacterial termination mechanisms.

concepts.title: Division of labor among RNA polymerases I, II, and III
concepts.rationale: The three-polymerase product map is directly tested in the teacher slides and is a classic single-best-answer topic.
concepts.summary: RNA polymerase I produces the 45S precursor that yields 18S, 5.8S, and 28S rRNAs. RNA polymerase II produces pre-mRNA and several regulatory RNAs. RNA polymerase III produces tRNAs and 5S rRNA, so the exceptional 5S product must not be assigned to polymerase I.
keyPoints: Pol I: 45S pre-rRNA → 18S, 5.8S, 28S.
Pol II: pre-mRNA and selected sn/miRNAs.
Pol III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.
Pol I acts in the nucleolus; Pol II and III act in the nucleoplasm.
clinicalLinks: α-Amanitin strongly inhibits RNA polymerase II and, at higher doses, polymerase III.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Transcription 2025.pptx, eukaryotic polymerase section.
Lippincott 6e, Chapter 30, eukaryotic nuclear RNA polymerases.

concepts.title: RNA polymerase II promoters and general transcription factors
concepts.rationale: The teacher slides test TFIIH, while Lippincott supplies the promoter and preinitiation-complex framework needed to understand it.
concepts.summary: RNA polymerase II does not recognize its promoter alone; general transcription factors assemble a preinitiation complex. TFIID, through TBP, recognizes the TATA box when present, and other core promoter elements can substitute in TATA-less genes. TFIIH opens DNA with helicase activity and phosphorylates the polymerase II C-terminal domain to permit promoter escape.
keyPoints: TATA/Hogness box is a core promoter element near −25 in many genes.
TBP is part of TFIID.
General factors position Pol II and create an open complex.
TFIIH has helicase and kinase activities.
clinicalLinks: Defects in TFIIH-associated nucleotide-excision repair/transcription proteins can cause xeroderma pigmentosum or trichothiodystrophy.
sourceEvidence: Teacher: Transcription 2025.pptx, Pol II general-factor section.

concepts.title: 5′ capping and 3′ polyadenylation of pre-mRNA
concepts.rationale: These modifications connect transcription to RNA stability, export, and translation and are core Lippincott Chapter 30 outcomes.
concepts.summary: Eukaryotic pre-mRNA receives a 7-methylguanosine cap through an unusual 5′–5′ triphosphate linkage early during transcription. The 3′ end is cleaved downstream of the AAUAAA signal and poly(A) polymerase adds a tail that is not directly encoded by the DNA template. The cap and tail protect the transcript, support nuclear export, and cooperate in efficient translation initiation.
keyPoints: The cap is 7-methylguanosine linked 5′–5′.
The cap supports stability, export, and ribosome recruitment.
AAUAAA directs cleavage/polyadenylation.
Poly(A) polymerase adds the non-templated tail.
Histone mRNAs are an important poly(A)-tail exception.
clinicalLinks: Mutations in polyadenylation signals can reduce normal mRNA production, including in globin disorders.

concepts.title: Spliceosome mechanism, splice-site disease, and alternative splicing
concepts.rationale: Splicing is indispensable for eukaryotic gene expression, and splice-site mutations are a common mechanism of inherited disease.
concepts.summary: The spliceosome uses snRNPs to recognize the 5′ GU site, branch-point adenine, polypyrimidine tract, and 3′ AG site. Two transesterification reactions form a lariat and join neighboring exons without consuming ATP for the bond-exchange chemistry itself. Alternative splice-site choice allows one gene to produce different protein isoforms, while pathogenic splice mutations can cause exon skipping, intron retention, or activation of cryptic sites.
keyPoints: Introns are removed and exons are ligated by the spliceosome.
The branch-point A forms a 2′–5′ bond in the lariat.
Consensus boundaries are usually GU at the 5′ end and AG at the 3′ end.
Alternative splicing expands the proteome without adding genes.
Splice-site mutations can alter the reading frame or introduce premature stops.
clinicalLinks: β-thalassemia can result from abnormal β-globin pre-mRNA splicing.
Antisense oligonucleotides can therapeutically redirect splicing in selected diseases.
sourceEvidence: Lippincott 6e, Chapter 30, spliceosome, splice-site mutations, and alternative splicing.

concepts.title: Transcription inhibitors as mechanism probes and drugs
concepts.rationale: Actinomycin D, rifampicin, and α-amanitin are named directly in the teacher transcription deck.
concepts.summary: Actinomycin D intercalates into DNA and broadly blocks RNA-chain elongation. Rifampicin binds the β subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase and prevents productive initiation. α-Amanitin from Amanita mushrooms most strongly inhibits eukaryotic RNA polymerase II, shutting down mRNA synthesis.
keyPoints: Actinomycin D targets DNA and inhibits transcription broadly.
Rifampicin selectively targets bacterial RNA polymerase.
α-Amanitin is most potent against Pol II.
Selectivity depends on whether the target is DNA itself or a domain-specific polymerase.
clinicalLinks: Rifampicin is a key antimycobacterial drug and a strong hepatic enzyme inducer.
Amanita poisoning can produce fulminant hepatic failure.
